claims.text: WHAT LAZAR CLAIMED, in his own 1991 narration. That stable superheavy elements exist 'in the 114 115 range which don't appear on a periodic chart' and that 'Beyond Element 115 the elements become unstable again and in fact element 116 decays in fractions of a second'. That 'the power source is a reactor which uses this element 115 as its fuel', with 115 'used as a Target and is bombarded with protons', a proton entering a 115 nucleus producing 'an atom of element 116 which remember decays instantly', radiating antimatter which is then annihilated for power. That 'only 223 grams of 115 which is just under half a pound can be utilized for a period of 20 to 30 years', that 'element 115's melting point is 1740 degrees Celsius', and that 'the element 115 is machined into triangles like this and is then inserted into the reactor'. Auto-generated captions at 18:42, 19:01, 23:31 and 25:34, so wording is approximate.

claims.text: THE LOAD-BEARING PHYSICAL CLAIM, which is the one the physics objections attack: 'The most important attribute of these heavier stable elements is that the gravity a wave is so abundant that it actually extends past the perimeter of the atom', and separately 'gravity a is what is currently being labeled as the strong nuclear force in mainstream physics'.

claims.text: WHAT THE CLAIM WOULD REQUIRE, STATED PRECISELY. An isotope of atomic number 115 with a half-life long enough to be produced in bulk, turned on a lathe into triangular wedges, stored, and consumed at a few grams a year across twenty to thirty years, which is a half-life of years at an absolute minimum and in practice geological. And a strong nuclear force whose range grows with nuclear mass until it reaches outside the atom. This is a stated inference from the claim's own terms and is marked Tier 3 as such.

claims.source: Oganessian et al., Physical Review C 69, 021601(R), 2 February 2004, https://journals.aps.org/prc/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevC.69.021601 , opened 2026-09-18
claims.text: WHAT WAS ACTUALLY SYNTHESISED. Element 115 was first reported in Oganessian et al., 'Experiments on the synthesis of element 115 in the reaction 243Am(48Ca,xn)291-x115', Physical Review C volume 69, article 021601(R), published 2 February 2004, a Dubna and Lawrence Livermore collaboration. The abstract reads: 'With a beam dose of 4.3x10^18 248-MeV Ca48 projectiles, we observed three similar decay chains consisting of five consecutive alpha decays, all detected in time intervals of about 20s and terminated at a later time by a spontaneous fission with a high-energy release (total kinetic energy ~220MeV). At a higher bombarding energy of 253MeV, with an equal Ca48 beam dose, we registered a different decay chain of four consecutive alpha decays detected in a time interval of about 0.5s, also terminated by spontaneous fission.' The isotopes are 288 and 287, at cross sections of roughly 3 picobarn and 1 picobarn.

claims.source: IUPAC, 'Discovery and assignment of elements with atomic numbers 113, 115, 117 and 118', 30 December 2015, https://iupac.org/discovery-and-assignment-of-elements-with-atomic-numbers-113-115-117-and-118/ , opened 2026-09-18
claims.text: A PRECISION POINT USUALLY GOT WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry assigned discovery priority for element 115 on 30 December 2015 to 'the Dubna-Livermore-Oak Ridge collaborations', and the basis given is work 'starting in 2010, and subsequently confirmed in 2012 and 2013, have met the criteria for discovery'. The priority statement therefore rests on the 2010 to 2013 work and not on the 2003 experiment. The Joint Working Party report is Karol, Barber, Sherrill, Vardaci and Yamazaki, Pure and Applied Chemistry 88 (2016) 155.

claims.text: The name moscovium, symbol Mc, was formally approved on 28 November 2016 and announced on 30 November 2016: 'Moscovium with the symbol Mc for element 115... proposed by the discoverers at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna (Russia), Oak Ridge National Laboratory (USA), Vanderbilt University (USA) and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (USA)', in recognition of the Moscow region.

claims.source: Physical Review C 69, 021601(R), 2 February 2004; and Emile Kinley-Gauthier, 'The Strange Case of Bob Lazar', Skeptic, 23 April 2026, https://www.skeptic.com/article/the-strange-case-of-bob-lazar/ , opened 2026-09-18
claims.text: THE COLLISION, STATED WITHOUT OVERSTATEMENT AND WITHOUT SOFTENING. Nothing about moscovium is stable, machinable, storable or available in gram quantities: it is produced one atom at a time at cross sections of about one picobarn and its decay chains run to completion within seconds. That is a direct contradiction of the claim's central requirement. It is NOT a refutation of the existence of element 115, which was never in dispute and was predicted long before 1989. Skeptic magazine's April 2026 treatment states the position correctly: IUPAC recognition 'does not validate Lazar's specific claims about a stable isotope or gravity propulsion'.

claims.text: THE PRIOR ART, WHICH CUTS AGAINST THE HOSTILE READING AS WELL AS THE CREDULOUS ONE. The island of stability near element 114 was mainstream, popularised physics well before 1989. Glenn Seaborg's article in Scientific American of April 1969, pages 57 to 67, carried graphics of expected half-lives for superheavy elements, and a 1970 chemistry textbook described element 114, with 114 protons and 184 neutrons, as 'an island of stability in a sea of instability'. A reader of popular science in the 1970s and 1980s had 114 and 115 available. The Seaborg article itself was not opened and is cited here only as Mahood cites it.

claims.text: THE PHYSICS OBJECTIONS, NAMED AND DATED. Dr David L. Morgan, a particle physicist, in 'A Physicist's Critique' of 26 August 1996, revised April 2001, makes three. First, on identifying gravity with the strong force: 'The strong nuclear force has NOTHING TO DO WITH GRAVITY... The equations and coupling strengths which describe the two forces are totally different and unrelated.' Second, on the force reaching outside the atom: 'The nuclear force extends out to about the same distance away from a nucleus NO MATTER HOW MASSIVE THE NUCLEUS IS. This fact is fundamental to the science of nuclear physics.' Third, and the one that does not depend on any model of gravity, an energy-conservation objection: if the antimatter must be manufactured on board by bombarding 115 with protons, the energy required equals the energy released on annihilation, so 'If you have to MAKE your own antimatter on board, your system produces NO NET ENERGY AT ALL!!'

desc: THIS NODE RECORDS A CLAIM AND A SEPARATE PHYSICAL FACT THAT HAPPEN TO SHARE A NUMBER, AND IT IS NOT AN ASSERTION THAT THEY ARE THE SAME THING. The claim is Lazar's: that a stable isotope of element 115 was the fuel of the reactor he says he worked on, that it could be machined into triangular wedges and stored, that 223 grams would run for twenty to thirty years, and that its nuclear binding field, which he calls gravity A and identifies with the strong nuclear force, extends past the perimeter of the atom so that it can be accessed and amplified. The fact is that element 115 was synthesised in a Dubna and Lawrence Livermore experiment published in Physical Review C on 2 February 2004, that the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry assigned discovery priority on 30 December 2015, and that the name moscovium was approved on 28 November 2016. The two do not meet. Lazar's claim is not that element 115 exists, which was never controversial and was predicted popular physics from 1969; it is that a stable isotope of it exists and that he handled half a pound of it. Nothing in the 2004 paper, the 2015 priority decision or the 2016 naming touches that. Equally, the hostile version, that he invented a number and got lucky, is also wrong: the island of stability near element 114 was in Scientific American in April 1969 and in undergraduate textbooks by 1970. The correct finding is neither prescient nor fabricated from nothing. It is available prior art, used. The board carries the claim as a claim and the element as an element, on one node so that the collision is visible in one place.

timeline.label: Physicist David L. Morgan publishes the physics critique
timeline.text: Dr David L. Morgan, a particle physicist, publishes 'A Physicist's Critique', revised April 2001. Three objections: that the strong nuclear force 'has NOTHING TO DO WITH GRAVITY'; that the nuclear force 'extends out to about the same distance away from a nucleus NO MATTER HOW MASSIVE THE NUCLEUS IS'; and, crucially without needing any model of gravity, that if the antimatter must be made on board then 'your system produces NO NET ENERGY AT ALL!!'

timeline.label: Element 115 synthesis published in Physical Review C
timeline.text: Oganessian et al., 'Experiments on the synthesis of element 115 in the reaction 243Am(48Ca,xn)291-x115', Physical Review C 69, 021601(R), a Dubna and Lawrence Livermore collaboration. The isotopes are 287 and 288, at cross sections of roughly 1 and 3 picobarn, observed as chains of consecutive alpha decays running to completion within about twenty seconds and about half a second. Nothing about them is stable, machinable or storable.

timeline.label: IUPAC assigns discovery priority for element 115
timeline.text: Priority went to 'the Dubna-Livermore-Oak Ridge collaborations', on the basis of work 'starting in 2010, and subsequently confirmed in 2012 and 2013'. A precision point usually got wrong in both directions: the priority statement rests on the 2010 to 2013 work, not on the 2003 experiment. The Joint Working Party report is Karol, Barber, Sherrill, Vardaci and Yamazaki, Pure and Applied Chemistry 88 (2016) 155.

timeline.label: Element 115 formally named moscovium
timeline.text: The name moscovium, symbol Mc, was formally approved on 28 November 2016 and announced on 30 November 2016, proposed by the discoverers at Dubna, Oak Ridge, Vanderbilt and Lawrence Livermore, in recognition of the Moscow region. This event is regularly presented as vindicating the Lazar claim. It does not: his claim requires a STABLE isotope that can be machined and stored, and no such isotope exists.
